title: Adaptive socket reuse and early-timeout safety for cross-SDK transports
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Goal: Provide consistent, low-latency defaults across Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs for connection pooling, TCP keep‑alive, and adaptive idle-socket reuse, while adding safety around 'early' request timeouts to avoid data corruption/lost streams.

Background: Teams have observed customer regressions where short per-request deadlines (user code) combined with aggressive connection reuse caused streaming responses to be truncated or retried incorrectly. Different language SDKs currently expose different knobs (connect/read/write deadlines, poolSize, idleTTL, keepAliveInterval) with confusing defaults. This ticket standardizes a cross-SDK ergonomics model and implements practical improvements and examples.

Success criteria / acceptance:
- New cross-SDK doc and defaults published showing recommended values for: connect timeout, request deadline, per-chunk read timeout (streaming), idle socket TTL, max pool size, and TCP keepalive probe interval.
- SDKs implement a "safe-early-timeout" guard: when a request times out but has an open streaming response with queued bytes at the SDK transport level, the SDK will attempt a graceful drain or mark the connection unhealthy rather than immediately reusing it for a new request.
- End-to-end tests across Python/TS/Go show fewer streaming truncations under simulated flakey networks (synthetic latency/jitter).
- Backward-compatible config: all new flags are opt-out and environment variables documented.

Out of scope: protocol-level server changes, Dedicated routing policies, or persistent KV cache behavior unrelated to connection lifecycle.

Workplan:
1) Draft cross-SDK ergonomics doc with recommended defaults and rationale.
2) Implement guard in each SDK transport to mark conn as 'do-not-reuse' when an early timeout happened during an in-flight streamed body.
3) Add a lightweight health-check counter and idle socket TTL heuristics to reduce head-of-line stalls when backend closes connections unexpectedly.
4) Add examples for Python, TypeScript, and Go showing typical production tuning for short-latency interactive apps and long-polling/streaming apps.
5) Run chaos tests (latency/jitter/connection resets) and collect telemetry.

Notes on ergonomics recommendations (draft):
- connect_timeout: 250ms for multi-region clients; 500ms if region selection might induce cold DNS/route.
- initial_request_deadline: 15s default for interactive completions; allow callers to set longer.
- per_chunk_read_timeout (streaming): 5s conservative default to break dead streams, with a reassembly/mark-unhealthy path to avoid reuse.
- pool_max_idle: 2 per CPU core, clamped to a max of 16 per process by default.
- idle_socket_ttl: 60s for normal workloads, 15s for bursty short-lived clients to avoid stale sockets.
- tcp_keepalive_probe_interval: 75s default; expose override.

Implementation notes:
- Python: patch requests/httpx transport wrapper to add per-chunk read watchdog and a _mark_connection_unusable() call that interacts with urllib3 connection pool.
- TypeScript: update fetch/undici adapter to attach a ReadableStream watchdog; when timeout occurs mid-stream mark Agent socket as draining and don't return it to pool.
- Go: enhance http.Transport's IdleConnTimeout/ForceAttemptHTTP2 and wrap Response.Body.Read to detect early timeouts and call CloseIdleConnections on that transport (or tag connection as bad).

Risk & tradeoffs:
- Marking connections as non-reusable increases short-term connection churn and some TCP/TLS handshake cost; mitigated by conservative heuristics and limiting churn to when mid-stream data was present.
- Changing defaults may affect legacy clients; everything must be opt-out and documented.

Links and artifacts: Confluence doc (draft): https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/SDK+Transport+Ergonomics, GitHub proposal PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/1045, Chaos test plan: https://internal.redwood.ai/chaos/sdk-transport-2026
